n: The bridegroom begins a poem praising his bride’s beauty. Her eyes behind her veil are gentle as doves, and her flowing dark hair is like a flock of black goats streaming down the hills of Gilead.

f.g: Hill country east of the Jordan River, known for its pastures.

n: Her teeth are white and even, like freshly washed sheep, perfectly matched with none missing.

f.g: Each tooth has its match — a complete, even set.

n: Her lips are like a scarlet ribbon, her speech lovely, and her cheeks behind her veil glow like the red of a sliced pomegranate.
Her neck is tall and dignified like David’s fortress tower, hung with shields. Her necklaces may be pictured as those shields.
He describes her beauty with images of gentle twin gazelles grazing among lilies — soft, graceful, and lovely.
He resolves to stay with her until morning, describing her as a fragrant hill of spices.
She is completely beautiful to him, without a single flaw. Paul uses similar language of Christ’s Church as His bride.

f.w: there is no spot in thee

n: He calls her to come with him from the high, wild mountains of the north — Lebanon, Amana, Senir, and Hermon — places of lions and leopards. He wants her safe by his side.

f.g: Senir, the Amorite name for Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9).
A peak in the Anti-Lebanon range.

n: She has captured his heart with a single glance. “Sister” was an affectionate term for a bride in ancient love poetry, not a family relationship.

f.g: A term of tender closeness common in ancient Near Eastern love songs.

n: Her love is better than wine, and her fragrance sweeter than any spice. He echoes the praise she first gave him (1:2).

f.w: better is thy love than wine

n: Her words are sweet as honey and milk, and her clothing smells like the cedar forests of Lebanon. “Milk and honey” recalls the promised land.
She is like a private garden, a sealed spring — pure and reserved for her husband alone. The image honors faithfulness and chastity.

f.g: A walled garden, protected from outsiders.

n: Her “garden” is full of choice plants — pomegranates, henna, and nard. Every good thing is found in her.
The list of rare spices continues — saffron, fragrant cane, cinnamon, myrrh, aloes. Many were costly imports, showing how precious she is.

f.g: A fragrant reed or cane, also used in holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23).
Fragrant aloeswood, not the medicinal plant.

n: She is a fountain that waters gardens, a well of fresh, flowing water like mountain streams from Lebanon — a source of life.

f.g: Fresh, flowing water rather than still cistern water.

n: The bride answers, inviting the winds to spread the fragrance of her garden and welcoming her beloved into it — a poetic picture of giving herself to him in marriage.

f.g: She now calls the garden his — her love is freely given.
